profile.name: Wari
profile.tagline: Ritual dance of Huari, Peru, blending pre-Inca and Spanish traditions.
profile.insight: In 1570, chronicler Cristóbal de Molina recorded the dance as Waritaki, marking its evolution amid Spanish cultural influence in Huari, Áncash.
profile.profile: Wari, or Huaridanza, is a ritual dance from Huari district in Peru's Áncash region, rooted in a pre-Inca agricultural festival and shaped by Spanish colonial influence. Traditionally performed by four dancers and two musicians playing pinkullo flute and wanqar drum, the dance features circular formations and rhythmic footwork including a light step called arrebato and a strong zapateo ending. Costumes include formal suits with floral shawls, embroidered knee pads with bells, and distinctive pink mesh masks with painted facial features. The music combines flute and drum patterns typical of northern Peruvian highlands.
profile.profile_long:
Wari, also known as Huaridanza or the Dance of the Knights of Huari, is a ritual dance originating from the district of Huari in the Áncash region of Peru. Its roots trace back to a pre-Inca agricultural festival called pocoy mita, which celebrated the arrival of the first rains between September and October. This festival involved dances dedicated to huacas (sacred places) and mallquis (ancestors), including the huaricu dance where deer skulls were used as wind instruments. With the Spanish conquest and evangelization campaigns, indigenous rituals were syncretized with Christian celebrations such as the Exaltation of the Holy Cross and the Virgin of the Rosary, both held in September and October, coinciding with the agricultural calendar. The dance was first documented in 1570 by the chronicler Cristóbal de Molina under the name Waritaki, reflecting its evolution through cultural blending.

The dance is traditionally performed during religious festivals honoring the Virgin of the Rosary, patron saint of Huari, and the Exaltation of the Cross, with occasional performances during the Virgin of the Assumption festival in Chacas. In the province of Pomabamba, a variant of the original Waritaki exists with distinct choreography and musical tempo, performed in towns such as Sihuas, Urpay, Taurija, and Pataz.

The ensemble typically consists of four dancers and two musicians called cajeros, who play the pinkullo flute and the wanqar drum. In some urban neighborhoods of Huari, the group may expand to eight dancers and include a captain or guide. Occasionally, two Pallas dancers from another local comparsa accompany the group. The choreography unfolds in three main parts: dancers move in circular formations, emphasizing rhythmic support on the fourth beat, followed by the arrebato, a light stepping movement, and concluding with the jaleo or zapateo, a strong foot stamping resembling a huayno fugue.

Costumes are formal and symbolic: dancers wear blue or black suits with white shirts and ties, covered by a floral shawl with fringes tied across the chest. A golden embroidered sash is worn on the right waist, and two handkerchiefs are carried in the jacket pockets. The head is covered with a white neck-sewn cloth called uma paño, leaving the face exposed but covered by a pink mesh mask painted with large eyes, eyebrows, mustache, and a small wool beard. The hat is a white toquilla straw hat with a raised front brim, decorated with a colored silk ribbon and an artificial flower crown mounted on a wire frame. Pants are rolled up to mid-calf, covered by black velvet gaiters embroidered with 35 to 40 bells each, symbolizing penitence and devotion. White gloves and a command baton with a silver or bronze dog-head handle and a leather whip complete the attire.

Musically, the dance is led by two cajeros playing the pinkullo, a four-holed wooden flute with a beak mouthpiece, and the wanqar, a large eucalyptus bark drum with animal skin heads, carried on the left shoulder and struck with a stick in the right hand. The musicians often craft their own instruments, requiring deep knowledge of materials. The musical pattern remains traditional throughout the dance, except during general dances when chuscadas—a regional variant of huayno—are played.

Wari remains a living tradition in Huari and surrounding areas, embodying a fusion of indigenous Andean and Spanish colonial cultural elements, performed with strict adherence to its ritual and festive contexts.

sections.origins_and_history: Wari originates from a pre-Inca agricultural festival called pocoy mita, celebrated in the Huari district of Áncash, Peru. It was documented in 1570 by Cristóbal de Molina as Waritaki and evolved through Spanish influence, blending indigenous and Christian elements. The dance is linked to the arrival of rains and religious festivals such as the Exaltation of the Holy Cross and the Virgin of the Rosary.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Traditionally performed by four dancers and two musicians, the choreography has three main parts: circular formations with rhythmic emphasis on the fourth beat, the arrebato (a light step), and the jaleo or zapateo (a strong stamping step). In urban areas, groups may include up to eight dancers and a captain. The dance ends with a zapateo resembling a huayno fugue.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music is performed by two cajeros playing the pinkullo flute and the wanqar drum. The pinkullo is a four-holed wooden flute with a beak mouthpiece, played with the left hand, made from waroma wood. The wanqar is a large eucalyptus bark drum with animal skin heads, carried on the left shoulder and struck with a stick. The musical pattern is traditional except during general dances when chuscadas, a regional huayno variant, are played.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear formal blue or black suits with white shirts and ties, floral shawls tied over the chest, golden embroidered sashes, and carry handkerchiefs. The head is covered with a white cloth called uma paño and a pink mesh mask painted with facial features. They wear white toquilla straw hats decorated with silk ribbons and artificial flowers. Pants are rolled up, covered by black velvet knee pads embroidered with 35-40 bells each. White gloves and a command baton with a dog-head handle and leather whip complete the attire.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Wari is performed during religious festivals honoring the Virgin of the Rosary and the Exaltation of the Holy Cross in Huari, as well as occasionally during the Virgin of the Assumption festival in Chacas. The bells on the knee pads symbolize penitence and devotion to the Cross. The dance reflects a syncretism of indigenous agricultural rites and Christian celebrations.
sections.regional_variants: A variant of the original Waritaki exists in Pomabamba province, differing in choreography and musical tempo, performed in Sihuas, Urpay, Taurija, and Pataz in La Libertad region.
sections.lineage: Wari descends from pre-Inca agricultural dances, incorporating Spanish colonial elements, especially from Christian festivals, forming a mestizo ritual dance unique to the Huari district.

profile.sacred_note: Wari is a ritual dance performed during religious festivals with symbolic penitential elements such as the heavy bells on knee pads; it should be respected as a devotional practice.

basic_steps: Form a circle with fellow dancers
Step lightly on the arrebato step, quick and rhythmic
Perform the jaleo or zapateo with strong foot stamping
Maintain rhythmic emphasis on the fourth beat
Conclude with a zapateo resembling a huayno fugue
teaching.rhythm: Rhythmic emphasis on the fourth beat with alternating light and strong steps
teaching.formation: Circular formation of four to eight dancers, sometimes led by a captain
teaching.level_notes: Beginners start with basic circular walking and simple foot taps, progressing to arrebato and zapateo steps

music_profile.sound_description: Music features the piercing, melodic tone of the pinkullo flute combined with the deep, resonant beats of the wanqar drum, creating a rhythmic pattern typical of northern Peruvian highlands.

movement_profile.footwork: Light stepping (arrebato) and strong stamping (zapateo) with rhythmic emphasis on the fourth beat
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Circular formations of four to eight dancers, moving in coordinated patterns
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Alternates between light quick steps and strong stamping, rhythmic and steady

claims.text: La huaridanza, también llamada danza de los caballeros de Huari, es una danza ritual de origen mestizo andino-español, originario del distrito de Huari, en el departamento peruano de Áncash.
claims.quote: La huaridanza, también llamada danza de los caballeros de Huari, es una danza ritual de origen mestizo andino-español, originario del distrito de Huari, en el departamento peruano de Áncash.

claims.text: En 1570, el cronista Cristóbal de Molina detalla que la danza tenía como nombre Waritaki, esta evolucionó a medida que la nueva cultura española se consolidaba en la región.
claims.quote: En 1570, el cronista Cristóbal de Molina detalla que la danza tenía como nombre Waritaki, esta evolucionó a medida que la nueva cultura española se consolidaba en la región.

claims.text: Está compuesta tradicionalmente de cuatro danzantes y dos músicos de flauta y tambor llamados cajeros.
claims.quote: Está compuesta tradicionalmente de cuatro danzantes y dos músicos de flauta y tambor llamados cajeros.

claims.text: La coreografía de la huaridanza tiene tres 'momentos' fundamentales: círculos, arrebato (paso ligero), y jaleo o zapateo (paso fuerte).
claims.quote: La coreografía de la huaridanza tiene tres 'momentos' fundamentales, en que los danzantes hacen el recorrido formando círculos, con la apoyatura rítmica en el cuarto compás, el arrebato, que es un paso ligero, y el jaleo o zapateo, con un paso fuerte a modo de fuga de huayno.

claims.text: El traje base es un conjunto de terno azul o negro, camisa blanca y corbata, con pañolón floreado, rodilleras con cascabeles, máscara de malla rosada, y sombrero de paja toquilla con corona de flores.
claims.quote: El traje base es una vestimenta formal compuesta por un conjunto de terno azul o negro, camisa blanca y corbata... el rostro es cubierto con una máscara de malla rosada... un sombrero de paja toquilla, blanco... una corona de armazón de alambre sujeta un arreglo de flores artificiales.

claims.text: La música es interpretada por dos cajeros con pinkullo, una flauta de cuatro orificios, y wanqar, un tambor grande de corteza de eucalipto.
claims.quote: Dos músicos, conocidos como cajeros, portan un pinkullo... y la caja o wanqar, membranófono hecho de corteza de eucalipto con parches de cuero de animal.

claims.text: La danza se presenta en las festividades de la Virgen del Rosario y la exaltación de la cruz en Huari, y ocasionalmente en la Virgen de la Asunción de Chacas.
claims.quote: Se presentan durante las festividades de la Virgen del Rosario... en la exaltación de la cruz... y, ocasionalmente, en la fiesta de la Virgen de la Asunción de Chacas.
